A study of this issue of Crown corporations is almost a microcosm. It is not a microcosm because it is larger than that, but it is almost an analysis, if you will, of what is fundamentally wrong with the situation in Canada. The Government is out of control. There is no sense in the country that we in Ottawa, the Government and Parliament, the people who have the responsibility which has been entrusted to them by the citizens of Canada, really know what is going on, are in control and have some sense of propriety with regard to the expenditure of taxpayers' money, some sense of responsibility, some sense of the future and a plan by which to address the many concerns of Canadians. This situation involving Crown corporations is exactly parallel. It is, as the Auditor General said, a subgovernment. In fact, in terms of employees it is larger than the bureaucracy. It is larger than the main Government. The situation is totally out of control.
My colleagues pointed out that Crown corporations can be created at will, at any time, by two or three people who are appointed, not elected. They have no mandate from anyone. They have been hired for certain jobs. They can create new corporations, obligate the people of Canada for the debts of those corporations and spend not just hundreds, thousands or millions of dollars, but, rather, billions of dollars without being held accountable to anyone. However, the people of Canada are responsible for making those payments.
If we are a democracy, then this problem must be addressed. The chronology has been gone over. The Auditor General made the statement in 1975 that the financial accountability and management of Crown corporations is out of control. From that observation came a study in 1977. It was not a bad study. From that came draft legislation which the Progressive Conservative administration introduced and intended to have passed. Since then, there has been nothing except a proliferation of new Crown corporations. The problem has become even worse. What has happened? Why has this problem not been addressed? Everyone who has examined it, including the

It requires the disclosure of information which sometimes one does not want to disclose. It requires that satisfactory procedures are followed and that is sometimes a little bit annoying. There is no question but that dictatorship, having to account to no one, is a far more convenient system by which to work for the person who has the power. It is a very convenient process for Government. It is a convenient repository for the party faithful, for people to whom the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the Party is obligated. As well, Maurice Strong and Joel Bell of the Canada Development Investment Corporation passed no Public Service Commission exam. We do not know their salaries. We do not know what they are doing on behalf of the people of Canada.
Ian Sinclair!

Those who assert that federal expenditures are out of control should quote the record of the past seven years.
The record, as he points out, shows that Government spending as a percentage of GNP has fallen from 20.5 per cent in 1975 to 16.2 per cent in 1981-82. The only reason he could get away with misusing figures this way is that he does not count the Crown corporations. He does not count the enormous growth outside the public accounts in Crown corporations. It goes out over the airways to Canadians to pass on the impression that somehow Government is restraining its expenditures.
It is a blatant falsehood. This is a way of avoiding fundamental checks and balances. Over the years procedures have been built up in Government to try to check the manner in which public funds are being spent. The whole Treasury Board bureaucracy was built up to do that. The private sector has its own mechanisms. What happens to Crown corporations? Neither of those.
As the Auditor General points out, he has been unable to find, and doubts the existence of any fundamental economic evaluation of the Petrofina purchase prior to its being made. In other words, there was no evaluation. They spent a whopping pile of money with none of the rudimentary analyses that would be required if that was a direct part of Government operating through normal Government bureaucracies, or none of the rudimentary requirements that would be necessary if that was a private corporation which had to seek private funding for that kind of purchase. Because they satisfy neither requirement, they get away with totally inaccurate and wasteful procedures.
What happened? Petrofina shares were trading about $50, $55 a share. They shot up to about $85 a share while the rest of the market stayed flat. There was no reason for that escalation in share prices. There was no fundamental difference in Fina in terms of having made any discoveries or its income statement suddenly getting out of line. The reason was that there was inside information. It is very clear. Some friends of Fina, Petro-Canada or the Liberal Party, the three possible sources, knew about this proposed purchase and takeover. They bought those shares between $55 and $80 and eventually sold them to Petro-Canada for about $120.
Vast illicit fortunes were made by either friends of Petrofina, Petro-Canada or the Liberal Party. It is beyond dispute that vast fortunes were made. The infamous Maurice Strong collected a $1 million brokerage fee for that deal, the man we are now rewarding by making chairman of the new Corporation. We do not know how much we are paying him to do that. We are not allowed to find out. We are merely the elected representatives of the people. That does not give us any right to information about Maurice Strong's salary from the Canadian Development Investment Corporation. We do know that his salary as Chairman of the Board of AZL Corporation was $20,000 a year, plus a consulting fee of $100,000 a year. The reason we know that is because in the United States that has to be made public. In Canada we pay him with taxpayers' money and we cannot find out that information.

We were told that the total for the Petrofina purchase was $1,450 million. That is what Petro-Canada told us in its press release. The Auditor General points out it is actually $1,700 million. If this is a democracy, and we insist that it become a democracy, we must have the right to examine their books to see what they are spending. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate and to say right off that I believe Crown corporations are a very proud extension of Canadian Government policy. I am personally pleased to rise now and offer a defence in the face of some of the scurrilous attacks we have heard from across the aisle. I believe that Crown corporations in general give us a flexible way to attack problems in this country, ways that the private sector cannot on its own find or follow. In addition, I believe we have seen an excellent pattern developing where we have been able to use Crown corporations to extend Canadian ownership over our own economy. I approve of that extended ownership and I am pleased to stand up today in support of it.
I think that Crown corporations provide a competitive force, a chance for the people of Canada to look at a vital part of our economy through the eyes of a publicly-owned, Government-controlled institution and to have some confidence that the industry as a whole is operating in a competitive and beneficial fashion. 1 do not think that those positive characteristics of Crown corporations have been brought out today by Members of the Conservative Party. Those Members should have started talking about these characteristics of Crown corporations.
I wish to quote from two columns that have appeared in The Globe and Mail recently. These are summaries of a recent speech given by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in Calgary. Mr. Michael Valpy, a columnist with The Globe and Mail, has had a couple of reactions to that speech. I quote from yesterday's column:
In its sum and rhetoric, it implies that Mr. Clark leads a party, no longer of traditional Canadian conservatives, but of nineteenth century liberals with a philosophy updated and imported cn bloc from the Reaganomics across the line.

-it made no mention of the finest traditional thought and action of Canadian conservatism . .. He-

Member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger) gave a us an excellent analysis of the behaviour of Tory Members in asking questions of the president of a Crown corporation which would have revealed vital secret commercial information. I think it equally important to note that the Tory Member who just spoke who went on about his love for Crown corporations in principle, once again brought out all the code words and secret attacks guaranteed to undermine the public's faith. We saw that in 1980. We saw the Tory Party talking about its dislike for PetroCan and the need to wind it up. speechtext: When the House rose at six o'clock the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) had the floor.

Before the recess, Mr. Speaker, I said the motion presented by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) provides an opportunity to consider the key safeguard of our parliamentary democracy, namely, the public accountability of the Government. I support the motion and I make the charge that the Government, under the current Prime Minister and indeed, under his Liberal predecessor, Lester B. Pearson, have, by planned and deliberate policy, endangered our democratic system by avoiding public accountability. One instrument of that evil and dishonest policy has been the use, or the misuse, and abuse of the Crown corporation.
Let me say very quickly that there is good reason and justification for the employment of the device of a Crown corporation in our democratic system and in our society. There are and will be circumstances and situations when an activity, service or enterprise can be governed, provided or operated by a Crown corporation. The people of Cape Breton in Nova Scotia were well served when a Crown corporation called Sydney Steel Corporation was formed by the Government of Nova Scotia to continue the operation of the Sydney Steel works after that black Friday in 1967 on which the plant was closed and thousands thrown out of work. But in the hands of a devious Government intent on avoiding public accountability and parliamentary processes, the same corporate device can be used to isolate an activity, service or enterprise that the Government desires to cover up and keep hidden from public view and censure.
Let me review very briefly the situation in Canada at present. We have almost 200 federal Crown corporations wholly owned by the Government of Canada. They account for gross expenditures exceeding $30 billion. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition rightly termed this corporate morass
Supply
"the underworld of Government"-a sea of organizations peopled by characters like Joel Bell, Jack Horner, Pierre Juneau and assorted Liberal hacks like Bill Mingo and Harrison McCain-the mafia of Government.
By comparison, the current revenues of all Canadian provinces total only $45 billion, and if you view only the Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, you will find revenue totalling only $3 billion, only one-tenth of the revenues that flow to our federal Government underworld. Let me record the fact that last year the revenue of Petro-Canada alone exceeded $2.7 billion. You could say that Petro-Canada has grown, in terms of revenue, to the size of the entire Atlantic area.
We know the problems that exist. 1 have mentioned some gross examples and the Auditor General has documented many more, but what is the answer? Fortunately, we have a relatively simple solution and it is endorsed by many knowledgeable people.
First, a Statute of the Parliament of Canada should be enacted that would legislate all the necessary requirements and processes to ensure full parliamentary and public accountability of Crown corporations. Second, there should be a careful review of all existing federal Crown corporations by a competent tribunal or parliamentary committee so that existing Crown corporations could, in some cases, be restricted or eliminated and in other cases abolished.
We have the statutory model already. It was mentioned in the motion introduced by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. When he was Prime Minister he introduced Bill C-27, so we could start immediately to resolve the problem. We could start with the enactment of the statutory provisions contained in Bill C-27, and we could start immediately on a parliamentary review of existing Crown corporations.
I said at the beginning of my remarks that I believe that the national Government should exercise a social conscience in the framework and context of the free enterprise system. The Government must support and foster the free enterprise system. It is that system that will produce the wealth and enable us to establish social programs, health care services and educational services required by the people of Canada. We cannot do that unless we have in place a viable private sector that can produce the necessary wealth to carry on and pay for the required services.
The Crown corporation, as advanced and operated by the Government of Canada, has been the nemesis of the private sector. Those corporations have taken over areas of activities that for decades, and indeed for the whole of this century, have produced the wealth that allows us to have one of the better social systems in the world.
Anyone who supports Crown corporations in his desire to oust the private sector, in the result will destroy our social

service system in Canada. When we in the Progressive Conservative Party rise to defend and support the free enterprise system, we take nothing away from the social service system that exists in Canada. In fact, we are supporting that very social service system. We are acting on a social conscience because the social service system cannot exist unless it is supported. The only support it can have is that which is produced by the private sector.
Of course, this is the problem which faces the New Democratic Party. It wants to spend, it wants to have wealth, but it does not provide the method of producing it. This is where we differ. We can have a viable and effective social program because we are willing to take the steps which are necessary to support financially such a program.
We have heard in this debate and will continue to hear a list of the sins of Crown corporations, but what we are faced with is the perception created by the Government of Canada in the public mind that Crown corporations are good. We know that the Government has the capacity and ability to create that perception in the public mind. But 1 challenge the people of Canada to check this year, next year and following years the performance of Petro-Canada. 1 challenge them to go to gasoline pumps across the land to see if they are getting a better deal from Petro-Canada than they are getting from even multinational oil companies which have no interest in Canada, in the economy of Canada or in the welfare of Canadians.
1 could take Mr. Speaker to places in Halifax, Nova Scotia, where side by side sit the private sector oil company and Petro-Canada, and the Petro-Canada prices are higher. How can Petro-Canada be accomplishing anything for Canadians? What is it doing? Time and time again I hear reports which indicated that Petro-Canada behaves not only like oil companies in the private sector but like the worst of those companies in the private sector. If, Mr. Speaker, you know any Petro-Canada dealers, you should just ask them whether they are required to take Petro-Canada products at higher prices than are available in Canadian department stores and that if they do not accept those products their franchises will be terminated.
I could go on and on, but the message must be given to Canadians so that they are aware of the evil of Crown corporations, just as they ought to be aware of the value of Crown corporations in certain circumstances.
That is why we are here. We are here to make the case, not against viable and valuable Crown corporations but against those Crown corporations which are destroying our private sector and hurting our economy and, in that very way, undermining the social service system in Canada. We have to counteract the activities of the Government in trying to create the idea across Canada and among Canadians that their action is intended to benefit the people of Canada, because in most
cases the action is only intended to benefit the welfare of the Liberal Party of Canada and those who support it.
1 want to end on a positive note. We can solve the problem very simply, as I said, by introducing legislation in the Parliament of Canada and by reviewing existing Crown corporations. In that way we will strike down the evil which has existed for past decades under the Prime Minister and his Liberal predecessor. Then we will end this cancer on our private sector, this cancer on our society which will not only destroy the free enterprise system but will destroy the social service system that is supported by free enterprise.

Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 am delighted to rise to speak in support of the motion which is before us today, and I hope the Official Opposition will feel the same about our amendment, because my party both practised and advocated accountability of Crown Corporations for something nearing 50 years. One of the things that I find strange and one thing we must get straight in the debate is that certainly since the First World War, the only time a Conservative or Liberal Government started a Crown corporation was when the so-called private sector could not or would not fill a public or national need or had gone belly-up, and successive Conservative and Liberal Governments ran to bail them out. They were not created because these Governments believed in them. Those were not really the best reasons for starting Crown corporations.
1 suppose the classic example is the Canadian National Railways, started by Sir Robert Borden, not because he believed in a publicly-owned railroad, but, rather, because the then Bank of Commerce and a number of other trust companies and bondholders were about to lose their money. Therefore, five bankrupt railroads were put together because free enterprise could not and would not work, could not and would not and did not make a buck, and could not and would not and did not serve the needs of this nation when it came to transportation. Therefore, Canadian National was formed, not in order to have a Crown corporation, but, rather, to have the people who had their private money invested bailed out and paid off and paid back. This country has been paying that private sector back tens and hundreds of millions of dollars ever since.
When I say that we have advocated and supported public accountability by Crown and private corporations for 50 years, I like to illustrate it by saying that we put our action where our mouths were and we did it. In the 1940s the then Premier Douglas in Saskatchewan established a Crown corporations committee and, from that day until now, every Crown corporation had to appear before the legislature to account for its annual reports, financial statements, operating practices, and management-labour relations practices, and they still do. I am not sure how long that will last with the present Government in my Province, but the proof is there. Similarly, in the Province of Manitoba, the then Premier, Mr. Schreyer, established a Crown corporations committee so that any Crown corporation must appear before the elected representatives and account for its annual report and all aspects of its activities. We should have the same here, in the Parliament of Canada.
I take a little pride in having had one of my amendments accepted by the Governent, practically the only one. The then Minister of Transport, Mr. Lang, accepted an amendment from me in the early 1970s when Air Canada was separated
Supply
from Canadian National, which made it statutory "that the annual reports for those two corporations shall"-not "may", but "shall"-"be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport". That should be the case with every federal Crown corporation. Their annual reports should be referred to the appropriate standing committee where the subject matter is the same or similar. No doubt there will be some Crown corporations which do not fit into present standing committees and their terms of reference, in which event we would need an additional standing committee of Parliament to which all those other Crown corporations would be referred. This would be necessary because no one standing committee could deal with the annual report and activities of every single Crown corporation, even if they met 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
The so-called free enterprise ideology, particularly American, has never fit well in Canada, even before 1867. Even the Conservatives recognize and know this. I was happy to hear the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) say today that there is a proper role for Crown corporations under the federal Government and on behalf of the people of Canada.
Free enterprise economics which ignores cultural, political, social and other human variables has as much in common with reality as a game of Parcheesi. Crown corporations exist in Canada because the kindergarten classroom theory of the marketplace of my free enterprise friends to my right, if nothing else, is really irrelevant, because of our geography, diverse heritage, location of our citizens, and our climate, where the goods are produced.
What might resemble a competitive market in densely populated Europe or in most areas of the United States would still be a natural monopoly in Canada. Our small markets, long distances and climate are the major reasons we have more Crown corporations in Canada than most other nations. As Herschel Hardin says in his book "A Nation Unaware":
Public enterprise in Canada is the direct result of the dilemma of Canadians with their small domestic market immediately next door to the Americans with their large market and manifest power. We did not choose public enterprise freely.
It was forced on to reluctant Liberal and Conservative Governments by American enterprise and expansion. In each case the project, such as railway construction, was undertaken as a reaction to and against American initiatives.
Public enterprise in this country started with the building of the Lachine Canal. It is the public sector which has provided most of the needed capital for national infrastructure and communications. Sir John A. Macdonald convinced Canadians to pay for the Pacific Railway because private enterprise could not raise the money. The Government set up Trans-Canada Air Lines because the private companies could not and would not do the job, even though they were invited to join in. A series of blunders, miscalculations and corruption of private railways since the nineteenth century would make our Crown corporations look good.

Canadian Pacific Railway was paid for, rescued and has since been subsidized by the Government. It has become known as a private enterprise triumph. Canadian National, which took over bankrupt private railways, is considered as a public enterprise failure. Without public investment in CPR, that corporation would never have shown a profit.
It was the Tories in Ontario who nationalized hydro. I am interested in some of the comments of Tory Members regarding Bill S-31 when earlier, the Ontario Conservatives nationalized hydro in order to prevent American capital from taking over the electrical generation and distribution. It was for that reason and that reason only.
In the past our country- has had the attitude that where profit is to be made, private enterprise should do the job, otherwise public enterprise should take over. If you are going to run an enterprise with good businesslike practices, any private enterpriser will tell you it is dumb to start up, take over or operate an enterprise that does not make a buck. For 120 years Liberal and Tory Governments have been saying, if it is not going to make money and we must have it, then make it a public enterprise, or Crown corporation.
We in the New Democratic Party, and before that in the CCF, said that if we are going to have Crown corporations, we should not just take over and operate those that lose money, but those that make money as well. The profits should either be injected into general Government revenues or used to support other necessary Crown corporations that are losing money.
Not surprisingly, the tax-paying public under successive Liberal and Tory Governments has been left with the mistaken impression that public enterprise loses money while private enterprise makes money. That is not by accident, but by design. Each national Government has done that since the First Crown corporation was established, not because they believed in it, their hearts were for it or they wanted to make money. That would fly in the face of the marketplace, the free enterprisers. It would fly in the face of the endeavours of their friends who support them, those who only make the bucks out of those things that make bucks and to heck with anything else the country might need.
Crown corporations are highly visible. Private corporations can hide their waste and bungling. If you have one share in Canadian Pacific and go to their annual meeting to try to get the kinds of answers that you as a part owner of that corporation feel you have a right to know, you could not do that. In Canada now you do not have the right to find out how much the president or chairman of the board of that corporation is paid. The only way to find out is through the embarrassing way of going to the United States Securities and Exchange Commission.
The way the Liberals and Tories have set up our Crown corporation system in Canada, a Member of Parliament, let alone an ordinary taxpayer, cannot find out what the new Chairman of the Board of Directors of Canadian National, the head of VIA Rail or any senior official of a Crown corporation is paid. It is interesting to hear the Tories complaining and
crying about the lack of accountability. How can you have accountability from a Crown corporation when the rules under which they operate are identical to those under which private corporations operate in this country? As a shareholder, you cannot get that kind of information from either a Crown corporation or private corporations.
There is a mythology about capitalism to the effect that if a Canadian buys shares, he will have a vote at the annual meeting and the mythology is that the management and board will be answerable to the shareholders. Liberal and Tory Governments have set up Crown corporations in the same way. As I said, our Crown corporations are highly visible. Mr. Speaker, when Crown corporations are made accountable, then they have to be more efficient and innovative. And there are some public enterprise success stories for which they did not get much, if any, credit. Canadian National, believe it or not, pioneered the diesel locomotive and set up our first national radio network. Where the heck was private enterprise?
Air Canada, as well as having a long list of world firsts, won the gold medal last year for efficiency in operations, savings in fuel consumption and employee efficiency, a medal recognized and selected by all the other international airlines of the world. It was the first airline in the world to prepare detailed specifications for a commercial jet transport and that was in 1946. Where was private enterprise?
In 1908, Ontario Hydro began construction of a 110,000 volt transmission line when the experts said that the current dogma and wisdom was that the maximum we could have was 60,000 volts. That was under a Conservative Government public enterprise, a Crown corporation, which led the whole continent. Where was private enterprise? Where were these private investors and risk takers?

That this House condemns the Government for its deliberate proliferation of Crown corporations accountable to the Government rather than to Parliament and the taxpayers who, in the words of the Auditor General, "have every right to consider themselves the principal shareholders of these corporations", and instructs the Government to immediately introduce a Bill substantially the same as Bill C-27 in the Thirty-first Parliament so as to make such corporations properly accountable to the people.
Now, I am glad to see the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) back in his seat because I hope he will learn something from this point forward as he made some very clear errors in the presentation he just made. He asked, what alternative do the Conservatives have? My colleague, the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) referred to that alternative very clearly in the Bill he put forward in the Thirty-first Parliament when the Conservative Government was in power. That is a clear alternative to this Bill, and I am going to come back to the comparisons that the Auditor General has made between that particular Bill and the Liberal legislation on the Order Paper which is clearly inferior, not in the judgment of the Conservative Members of Parliament but inferior in the judgment of an independent and expert observer, the Auditor General.
While I am referring to the Hon. Member for Laurier, 1 might just correct one of the misstatements he made in his remarks with reference to the fact that the creation of subsidiaries will be brought before this Parliament for that tremendously important and extensive three-hour debate. I think he has learned from my colleague that there is no debate on the creation of subsidiaries. So if the CDIC is going to go out and buy Noranda or General Motors, if they have the funds in the till-and they could have the funds through the sale of the Canada Development Corporation-they can go ahead and create new Crown corporations with no further reference to Parliament.

December 9, 1982
Supply
That is the point we have consistently underlined as being a loss of control by Parliament. The Hon. Member for Laurier, the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) and other Members of Parliament will have no control over the creation of these subsidiaries. But none of the Liberals have directed their comments to the motion 1 have just read; none have defended the Government's position on Bill C-123 referred to in the motion. Perhaps I should say, with the possible exception of the Minister himself, but the defence he put up was really a laughable one. Now, that is not an uncommon occurrence in the remarks of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray). But none of the other Members has talked about the problems of accountability, control and financial reporting. It must be quite transparent to those people who are observing this debate that the Liberals cannot win this debate. They know they cannot win this debate, so what do they do? They distort the facts, they try to divert people's attention from the motion at hand. There is no logical argument coming from them as to why Bill C-123 is better than the Clark Government proposal. There is no alternative that they are talking about for Bill C-123, which they do not want to mention. It is clear today that when they do not have a defence they start talking about something else, and that has been very clear, from every Member of Parliament from the Liberal side.
As you are doing now.
I am coming to the point of the motion, and I will talk about this in a very clear and incisive fashion, unlike the Member from Newfoundland.
That will be refreshing.

The economy today is in a steep slide. Unemployment is running at 1.5 million people; bankruptcies are at record levels; the federal Government's deficit is at $24 billion and growing. The Government has consistently tried to shift the blame to the private sector, to the Central Bank in the United States, to the international economy, to all sorts of things. It has steadfastly refused to accept the blame for the problems we have today.
On Tuesday we were presented with the Report of the Auditor General, and Members of Parliament in that Report got a clear example of the alternatives that are open to the Government to address the problems, to free up funds, by better control of Crown corporations, by better control of the Government itself, funds that could be used to finance other programs of the Governement, reduce the deficit or whatever the Government wishes to do. But there are alternatives presented in this Report.
In the report the Auditor General highlights a huge sector of Government which he refers to as:
-an enormous iceberg, floating lazily in the foggy Atlantic; silent, majestic, awesome.
That is the subject of the debate tonight, Mr. Speaker, the adequacy of control and the accountability of that great, sleepy iceberg, the Crown corporations.
The message of the Auditor General's Report is that there is waste, there is a lack of control and there is inadequate accountability of Crown corporations. If this were reduced we would have considerable flexibility to address the problems at hand rather than being in the strait-jacket that this Government finds itself in now. Time and again the Government has said that nothing can be done, but clearly this Report shows us how things can be changed.
The response from the President of the Treasury Board, both today in the House and when the Report was brought down earlier this week, was typically weak and inadequate. He said, "The Report is useful; we are going to have to study it; we will have some comments once we have had a chance to study this Report." Just another study! That is not good enough.
This Report is a call for action, and Members of Parliament have a responsibility to take that action. This is a powerful indictment of Government inaction over the past five or six years. The Report sets out a number of initiatives that have been proposed by various individuals, by the Members of the Government opposite, as well as the people in the private sector, indicating ways that this accountability can be improved upon. But I stress the point that the history of this Government has been to shuffle that information aside, not pay adequate attention to it and not take strong enough action to direct itself at these problems.
The key objective and the key recommendations in the past, and in this Report, is the need for an over-all legislative framework. That is clearly set out in the Auditor General's Report, and we responded to that in the Clark Government by presenting the legislation that is referred to in the Auditor General's Report in 1979.
To have the President of the Treasury Board try to take credit for that legislation by saying it was based on some work initiated by the previous Liberal Government is a joke. We see clearly in the Auditor General's Report that they have taken a major step back in a number of areas from the position that was taken in the legislation put forward by the Clark Government.
I want to read something from the Auditor General's Report at page 57, Sections 2.50 and 2.51.
Although Bill C-27, the Clark Government Bill:
-had a number of deficiencies, it represented a major step toward a comprehensive and effective framework for the control, direction and accountability of crown-owned corporations. It also responded to-
-a number of recommendations, et cetera.
In the next paragraph it says:
Part V of Bill C-123 does not take the same comprehensive approach as did Bill C-27. Instead, it addresses only issues which the Government presumably believes demonstrate the most pressing need for correction.
On the next page, on page 58, it does a comparative analysis in a number of areas of the initiatives in those two pieces of
December 9, 1982

legislation against the general accountability framework that the Auditor General felt was important. Of the 33 areas in which they wanted action taken, the Clark Government acted on 25 in a full sense and partially on one. In Bill C-123 it was a very pitiful action on seven and partial action on two.
There is no comparison whatsoever, and for the President of the Treasury Board to take credit for it and to say that the piece of legislation that he has put forward, Bill C-123, is an adequate response to the requirements of the Auditor General, is a joke.
The understatement of the year is also on page 57 of the Auditor General's Report when he expressed disappointment that the legislative framework had not been provided.
I am sure that the Auditor General is bitterly disappointed that this proposed legislation is so inadequate. We as Members of Parliament should also be bitterly disappointed because we have a clear responsibility to take action here, to take the Auditor General's Report as an action plan, to bring forward legislation that is needed to control the taxpayers' money invested in Crown corporations.
Bill C-123 in my judgment is a sham. What it is doing is trying to put the Government in a position of being seen to be doing something when time and time again we have seen they are not taking the action that is required of them. That is why we are here this evening. We are not talking about an insignificant part of Government here. Using the Auditor General's words, "A sub-Government employs more people than Government Departments do as a whole." They spend $30 billion of taxpayers' money, but what is key is the scope of the Crown corporations throughout our economy. We all know about Canada Post, CN, Air Canada, the Bank of Canada, CBC and so on. But let us look at another few of these Crown corporations: National Battlefields Commission; Northern Power Corporation; Canadian Saltfish Corporation; Canadian Arsenals Limited; Defence Construction (1951) Limited; Canadian Dairy Commission. They are in all parts of our economy and it is important that we understand what is going on in these parts of the economy, and whether the moneys are being used effectively.
The authorization and mandate for Crown corporations is clearly too loose. There is too little control here. That has been touched on by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Welling-ton-Dufferin-Simcoe. But let me just comment on this Canada Development Investment Corporation again, to which the Member for Laurier referred. It was incorporated without adequate parliamentary review, it was incorporated earlier this year but there was no parliamentary approval. There was a fanfare, a press release and the appointment of Liberal backroom boys to top management positions, but there was only an Order in Council to transfer the objectives of the Canada Development Corporation to this new corporation. It was also made an agent of the Crown. That means that any time it borrows money, it borrows on the credit of the taxpayer. The taxpayer is directly obligated to stand behind those loans. That was done without parliamentary approval. Clearly, Bill C-123 is inadequate.
Supply
1 want to quote from the Auditor General's Report at page 62 where he said:
Because CDIC has objectives virtually identical to those of CDC allowing it to participate in almost any activity, it has the potential to acquire and dispose of business interests without parliamentary approval.
Let me give another example of why 1 am worried about this whole matter. Crown corporations today are not adequately controlled by Ministers. In the Clark Government I was responsible for the Export Development Corporation. Shortly after I took on that responsibility I initiated monthly meetings with senior management of EDC. After the second meeting the President of the Corporation said, "Congratulations, you just had twice as many meetings as your predecessor had." 1 had been there for two and a half months, Mr. Speaker, and he had been there for two and a half years at that time.
The point is not that 1 was doing such a great job. The point is that I was taking an interest and the other Minister had not taken any interest. It was a nuisance to him. He was letting that very important corporation float along without adequate ministerial control.
The Auditor General has said that broader, stronger parliamentary control and accountability is necessary-and that is absolutely the right conclusion-as Ministers are not exercising this. He says that their primary concern is the Department under their responsibility. The Crown corporation is a diversion, and that is why we must return to Bill C-27 introduced by my colleague so that Parliament can take over some of these responsibilities from the Ministers if the Ministers are not going to do the job.
There is one other step that I believe is important, Mr. Speaker, and that is to require each new Government, when it comes into office, to provide a written mandate to each Crown corporation within a certain period of time after it takes office. This written mandate would establish clearly what the Crown corporation was to do. These mandates change. They are written in a vague way in the incorporating legislation. Time passes, Governments change and so the interpretation changes. The best example of that is Petro-Canada, as mentioned in the Auditor General's Report. When it was incorporated there was no intention whatsoever that it would own service stations. Now the taxpayers have seen $2 billion of their money going to buy a series of service stations across the country.
Good!

It is not good. Let me point out why we have a problem with control of Crown corporations. If the Ministers do not take control of these Crown corporations then the bureaucrats take control. If there is one thing that 1 have heard time and time again in my travels in my constituency and across the country, it is that the bureaucrats have too much control and that there is not sufficient accountability to see that these corporations are run efficiently.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, let me say that the Government is moving down a very dangerous road if it ignores the advice of

the Auditor General and the legislation introduced by my colleague. After delaying for three years it has finally addressed the problem but in a totally inadequate way. The Auditor General has clearly said that the legislation is not good enough. Members of Parliament have a responsibility to their constituents and to taxpayers to listen carefully to the advice of the Auditor General. It is his responsibility to report directly to Parliament and not through a Minister. It is the responsibility of Members of Parliament to respond to the Auditor General. We must resolve today to force the Government to change this legislation. The taxpayers of Canada will accept nothing less.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if the hon. gentleman would entertain a short question.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member can only accept a question with the unanimous consent of the House because his time has expired. The Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's.

Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with great interest to the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). Among other things he said that no Liberal Member has spoken about the motion. I will do that very directly, Mr. Speaker. Let us see what the motion says.
We will help you with the big words.

The motion put down by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) reads in part as follows:
That this House condemns the Government for its deliberate proliferation of Crown corporations accountable to the Government-
There is the sin, Mr. Speaker, "corporations accountable to the Government". Is that not an awful crime, that the legitimately elected Government of this country should have organizations or corporations accountable to it that are under its control and direction? I always thought it was a function of Government to be in charge of the way the taxpayers' money is spent, whether through Crown corporations or otherwise. But there is the indictment. There is the reason we ought to be hanged. Out there we have Crown corporations which are accountable to the Government. That is our crime. That is the sin we are accused of today by the Hon. Member for Yellow-head.
Hon. Members opposite have run out of ideas. On this, their last Opposition day, this is the best they can do-accuse us of doing our job. They accuse us of making Crown corporations accountable to the legitimately elected Government of this country.
That is count one in the indictment, Mr. Speaker. There is evidence to show that we are absolutely guilty of that charge. As late as June of this year the then President of the Treasury Board took the dastardly step of making those Crown corporations even more accountable. On June 30 he introduced the Bill on Crown corporations. I wish my friend, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre had read it and understood it. The Bill provides very clearly for additional accountability to the
people who have been charged with the Government of this country.
The Bill provides for a number of legislative changes, organizational changes and administrative changes, all aimed at enabling the Government to act quickly-there is the sin- and responsibly in enhancing the relationship between the Government and the Crown corporation. It also charges the Government with responsibility to provide for the over-all capability of Government to act as a vigilant and effective shareholder in relation to its wholly-owned corporations. That is the crime, Mr. Speaker. That is what they have been talking about over there today, that is what they are talking about over there tonight. They complain that we have a system of Government in the country-a government endorsed by the people and legitimately elected by the people-which insists on Crown corporations being accountable to it in ever more rigid form, especially when we implement this new legislation. That is our crime, but it is not the full crime.
The Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead went on and on and on as he usually does. In his motion he indicated further:
-and instructs the Government to immediately introduce a Bill substantially the same as Bill C-27 in the Thirty-first Parliament-
There is a good idea. On the surface that is an excellent idea. We could go back to the thirty-first Parliament. That, for those who have chosen to forget-and there are many in the country who have chosen to forget that Parliament-is the Parliament during which the Tory regime had that brief interregnum in power.
Yours was even briefer, Roger; yours was only one day.
Oh, they are hurting now; they are even waking up over there.
You do sound like an alarm clock.

Yes, they are waking up, they are hurting. The Thirty-first Parliament had not only a Bill C-27; it had another Bill about which I want to tell the House. On the surface the idea of the Hon. Member for Yellowhead is a good one. I commend it to the Government and to the House. We ought to go back to the Thirty-first Parliament and have a look at the legislation put down by the Conservative Government. In fact, we looked not only at Bill C-27 but we looked at another one. I give notice now to the Official Opposition that we on this side of the House have the full intention of giving them the opportunity to vote for another Bill which they had on their Order Paper. We will let them vote for it word for word, dot for dot, every last comma, as it was. The Bill in its new form, the Bill under its new number, is a Bill which my friends on the other side of the House will recognize very well. They did not write the Bill but they brought it into the House. It happened to die on the Order Paper like they did.
When this Government came back into power after February 1980, we had the courage to resurrect that excellent piece
December 9, 1982

of legislation which the Tories had had on the Order Paper. We will give those people the full opportunity at third reading to vote for that particular Bill. The Bill is Bill C-10. 1 mention it tonight in order to draw a parallel with the suggestion of the Hon. Member for Yellowhead concerning Bill C-27. He said that we should go back, get Bill C-27 and bring it in because it is a good Bill. We have taken his advice on Bill C-10.
Does the House know what happened as soon as we brought it in without changing a comma? Those who were for it in the Thirty-first Parliament were suddenly "agin it". They have gone across the country and have written clergymen in the country, spreading fear that the state is going to take over religion. Where do they get the basis for that charge? In Bill C-10. What is Bill C-10? It is a piece of legislation under another number which was the identical piece of legislation the Tories brought in when they were in power.
Shame.

If the Hon. Member for Yellowhead wants us to have a look at Bill C-27, we will want every Member on that side of the House to put in writing that they promise not to do a 180-degree turn on Bill C-27 as they did on Bill C-10.
You got it, let's bring it in.

We want them to promise not to play cheap politics with Bill C-27 as they did with Bill C-10. We want them to promise not to go around the country spreading fear in the minds of the clergy, religious organizations and charitable organizations. We want them to promise not to be hypocritical on Bill C-27 as they were on Bill C-10. Give us that promise-
You have got it.

I see the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). It looks like he has dined very well again tonight. If he would only feed his mind half as well, what a man he would be.
This motion says more, although not a lot more. First it says that Crown corporations are accountable to the Government. 1 plead guilty to that sin. That is right. They are accountable, and we are making them even more accountable. The Government was elected to protect taxpayers' money.
How?
Read the Bill.
You read the Bill.
1 have read it. Which page would you like me to recite?
Never mind the page. What does it say?

I know it is tender for my good friend. Somebody called him-I would not do it, being that kind of an individual-the "honourable fat cat from Bay Street". I said, "No, that is not fair". I saw him tonight as the champion of the public purse. It boggles the mind-someone from Bay Street protecting the public purse. It is something like having an arsonist as the new fire chief, I suppose.
Supply
Or Marc Lalonde in charge of the economy.

What are those tyrannical things called Crown corporations, these insidious things creeping out there in the country and destroying us all? We have such monsters as the National Battlefields Commission! There is a lot of scope for skulduggery and mischievousness! Imagine the damage it could do to the country if it were allowed to really get loose-the National Battlefields Commission! Then there are the International Joint Commission and Hockey Canada Inc.
Perhaps if the truth were known as to what is bothering them, it would be a Crown corporation called Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada ought to be a fond term in the minds of every Tory in the country because that is a subject they know well, both sides of it, because they have been on both sides of it. During the election campaign they were for privatizing it, but then they learned that that might not be the thing to do, so they did a Petro-Canada trip similar to the Jerusalem trip.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They took a poll.

Yes, they took a poll and for once they understood a poll. Then they said that perhaps they should not be for privatizing it at all, that perhaps they should keep it much as it is, somewhat like it is, maybe all like it is. They got the message and found that corporations such as Petro-Canada, the National Battlefields Commission, the International Joint Commission, Hockey Canada Inc. and Fashion Canada, were not the creeping monsters which they had conjured up in their minds. It must have been terrible for them to live with it every day. Every waking moment they must be shaking because they think one of those monsters, one of those Crown corporations, will get them by the throat somewhere. What a terrible thing to have to carry around with them, those poor, poor Tories.
Perhaps they are concerned about a couple of corporations with which I have had reason to deal. Perhaps it is the Canadian Saltfish Corporation. There is a villain, there is an absolute monster! Among other things it has its headquarters in Newfoundland. Have we heard about the damage it has done to this country? In all the time it has been there as a corporation, does the House want to know how much money it has received to bail it out, money from the Treasury of the country? How much money has Parliament voted to keep that outfit alive so that it could squander more of the taxpayers' money on behalf of fishermen in Newfoundland, part of Quebec and so on? Do Hon. Members want some idea of how much money? Not one red cent, not one red cent. They do not bother to tell you that some companies out there are making a few bucks for the Treasury. They do not bother to tell you that some of the Crown Corporations which they want to malign and undermine and soil the reputation of, and belittle, are doing a good job on behalf of the fishermen in this country. If people live too far West to know about the Saltfish Corporation, let me tell

Supply
them about another, the Canadian Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation which has its headquarters in Winnipeg, just west of Thunder Bay. That, too, has taken a big fat nothing out of the Treasury. That corporation also has committed the heinous sin of going without funds from this Parliament.
There are a couple of corporations serving this country well. J could tell you about several more, in fact, many many more, Mr. Speaker, but Hon. Members over there do not want to hear about them.
Start naming them.

That is why they keep bawling and yapping on the other side because they do not want to hear that the corporations of this country are answerable to the legitimately elected Government of this country, and, by and large, are doing a good job.
Hear, hear!
1 said by and large because I, like any person in this House, have a few scores to settle with a Crown Corporation like CN Marine.
And Canada Post.
There are a few with Air Canada I can settle.
Nationalize them then.

But this is not the place to settle those scores. We might have individual beefs. I hear Members on the other side. Maybe they did not have the right kind of wine one night on the first class flight, but that does not mean we should wipe out the whole corporation-maybe the President, yes.
Get rid of the President because he is not a Grit.

Seriously, we ought to recognize once in a while that you cannot, day in and day out, get your jollies or get your kicks out of raking everybody and everything down. The Crown Corporation has served this country well. If there are some imperfections, as I am sure there are, as there are with any organization established by man-
Or women. Quit being a sexist.
The Hon. Member has learned a new word tonight. He does not understand it but he has learned it.
Oh, oh!
The Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre quoted rather extensively from the Auditor General's Report. Well, two people can play that particular game. Somewhere in these pages-
Why don't you get someone to turn the pages for you?
-the Auditor General also goes on to point out very clearly-
You had better drink to that.
1 will drink to that as long as it is water.
Oh, oh!

The Auditor General points out something else very clearly on the same page as the page my hon. friend for Etobicoke Centre quoted from. I might say quoted selectively and conveniently. It is pointed out in the Report by the Auditor General how the Crown Corporations have a legislative base; how Parliament has a way of making those corporations accountable. I say to the Hon. Member, and I say to his Leader who put down this motion, that the problem with their logic and their approach on this particular issue is the same as their approach on any problem. They go at it back-foremost. They are coming at it from the wrong end. They would do well to read all of the Report before picking out convenient little bits. 1 would suggest Hon. Members over there have never read it at all. They ran to the newspaper this morning to get the juicy bits and figured they had a good thing going.
Have you read it, Roger?
A few pages to go.
Oh, oh!

A few pages to go. 1 say to the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre, who has the great reputation for being a man from Bay Street, a man who understands business, that he does his reputation no good at all to be associated with a group of people who are on this witch hunt of "How much is so and so paid; how much is that person's salary?"
Why shouldn't we know that?
If you ask questions, you might get answers.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member's time has expired. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn).

Mr. Speaker, it is always entertainment to the House to hear the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) speaking about his National Battlefields Commission. We were most impressed by the costs of SaltFish Corporation and the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, but what he fails to realize is that the shareholders of Canada, the people of this country, represented by Members in this House, are entitled, as shareholders in these corporations, to demand an accounting from the Corporations and their executive. They are entitled at least once a year, like any other shareholders of any other corporation, to demand an accounting from the president and the executive officers of the Corporation. It has been the habit of this Government to hide as much as it can. It is a situation of "bury it under the carpet and make sure it is never shown".
December 9, 1982

This Party on the other side of the House, this Liberal Government, is a master at hiding, burying and shoving things under the table.
We have, as the Auditor General says, a sub-government that looks after well in excess of $30 billion in transactions a year, and we as the representatives of the people cannot look, cannot see, cannot ask about them because the Government wants to keep the information buried under the table, and this Government wants to do its borrowing in one way or another and its manoeuvring in one way or another. This Government does not want the people to know what it is doing. That is the issue, and that is the issue the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's and the entire Liberal Party runs away from. That is what this debate is about tonight.
I refer to two business Crown Corporations that have recently been transferred under the blanket of the Canada Development Investment Corporation, under the hideout controlled by the Minister of State for Social Development, of all things, Senator Austin from the other place. He is a Minister who says he does not know what Canadair and de Havilland are all about. A Minister who is taking over control of these Corporations says, just as the Auditor General said, "I do not know how much money they are going to need. I know that the $200 million that we are asked to vote for each of them tonight is not enough." He said, and he said it in testimony given to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, that the amount will last maybe until March. They will then need at least $100 million and maybe more than that by March. We are asked to vote in favour of spending more money when we, as Members of Parliament, as representatives, as shareholders of these corporations, cannot get an accounting.
Let me deal first with Canadair. Canadair is the subject of the Auditor General's Report. In his Report, dealing with the last fiscal year of this Government's operation, he indicated that the $1.35 billion authorized in loans to that corporation was not sufficient. It clearly was not sufficient because the Government is coming to us tonight to demand another $200 million for that corporation. The Minister of the Government who is responsible for the Canada Investment Development Corporation has said in committee that that is not enough. I say that the people of Canada have a right to know where we are going. Where are we going? Where is the Government taking us? Where is it spending the money of the people of Canada? It is as simple as that. It is not a question of whether we should build a Challenger jet or whether we should own an aircraft corporation. It is the basic right to know where we are going. What are the projections for sales? How is this management operating?
Let us discuss management for a while. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), in his other capacity as Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce before the latest shuffle, wrote two letters to the present Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), previously the President of the Treasury Board. Both of those letters are available for public scrutiny because they were leaked to us. In each of those
Supply
letters, the present President of the Treasury Board, that great squanderer of the people's money, said that Consolidated Computer needed a little more money, another $25 billion, another $35 million. Indeed, while he was Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, he deliberately allocated over $50 million of money to Consolidated Computer, and then the lid blew off. Then we gave away that company for the sum of $1 and we sold nearly $50 million worth of assets for $100,000.
If the Parliament of Canada had had an opportunity to review Consolidated Computer annually, the Government and the people of Canada would not have lost $125 million, but it was hidden. It was swept under the carpet by a Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who wanted to protect himself, and it really did not matter to him whose money he was spending. After all, the money comes from the great money tree and the Government spends it and shuffles it here to try to cover up the losses, and the Auditor General points that out.
To say, for one moment, that the House should not have some control over the business activities conducted by the Government, under the guise of a Crown corporation, is to say that Members of Parliament have no right to examine the spending of the people of Canada. Sir, the barons of Run-nymede did not put up with that with King John. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this House cannot put up with this kind of activity.
Representatives of Canadair appeared before our committee for two and one-half hours. During that time, the executives of that corporation refused to disclose their projections, refused to disclose their creative bookkeeping methods, refused to set out the costs of building an airplane, refused to say how many airplanes they had to build to get the company out of debt and refused, indeed, to give us any of the details. This Party asked for in camera hearings of the committee so that ordinary commercial matters would not be disclosed to the public, but the Government refused to give us those in camera hearings because it somehow wants to keep the lid on it all. Well, the Auditor General has blown their cover. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada will blow its cover when an election comes, because we cannot put up with this kind of failure to disclose and this failure of responsibility any longer.
Hear, hear!
